title: Narrator's Point of View
keyIdea: The narrator is the voice that tells a story. In first person the narrator is a character who says I or we, so you only learn what that one person sees, thinks and feels. In third person the narrator stands outside and says he, she or they; an all-knowing third-person narrator can show many characters' thoughts. Words inside speech marks do not change who is narrating. When two narrators tell the same event, each chooses what to include and leave out, so the story feels different.
familyTip: Pick a page from a book your child is reading and ask: who is telling this story? Look for I or we outside speech marks. Then retell a family event twice: once as I, once as a narrator who can see into everyone's head. Ask what changed and what each version left out.

visual.caption: First or third person? Drag each sentence, or tap it and then a box.

items: "I give up," Max sighed, and he sat down.
The children stared at the sky.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort sentences by narrator, switch narrators to read minds, retell in third person, compare two tellings and choose narrators.

kid: Every story has a narrator. The narrator is the voice telling the story. It is not always the author. Ask yourself: who is telling this?

In first person, the narrator is a character in the story. They say I, me, my and we. You see everything through their eyes. You hear their thoughts. But they cannot see inside anyone else's head. They can only guess from faces, words and actions.

In third person, the narrator is outside the story. They call the characters he, she and they. Some third-person narrators follow one character. Others know everything and can tell you what every character is thinking. Be careful with speech marks. In "I'm hungry," Tom said, the I belongs to Tom. The narrator is still outside the story.

The narrator changes what you know. If Sam tells the story of a smashed window, you hear about the wind and his worry. If Mrs Patel tells it, you hear about her curtains and that Sam ran off. Authors pick first person to make you feel close to one character. They pick third person to show more people and places.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. This matches CCSS RL.4.6: compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrated, including the difference between first- and third-person narration. In England it supports Year 5 and 6 reading, where pupils discuss how authors use language and structure to shape the reader's view.

Useful terms. A first-person narrator uses I or we and is limited to their own perceptions; they may be unreliable. Third-person limited stays with one character's thoughts. Third-person omniscient can enter any mind and move freely in time and place. Second person (you) is rare in fiction for this age and is left out here. Narrator and author are different people: the author chooses the narrator.

Common mistakes to watch for. Many children label any sentence containing I as first person, even when the I is inside dialogue. Others think the narrator must be the main character, or that a first-person narrator knows what others feel. When retelling in third person, a frequent slip is changing pronouns inside speech marks too, or changing only some of them so two narrators are mixed. Ask: who is telling, and how could they know that?

practice.prompt: "Hurry up!" Ava called, and she grabbed her coat. Which point of view is this?
practice.hint: Look outside the speech marks. What does the narrator call Ava?
practice.explain: The narrator says she and her, so this is third person. The words in speech marks are Ava talking.

practice.prompt: A first-person narrator says: "Leo looked angry." Why does she say looked?
choices: She can only guess from his face
practice.hint: Can one person see inside another person's head?
practice.explain: A first-person narrator only knows her own thoughts. She sees Leo's face and guesses how he feels.

practice.prompt: In a first-person story, {n} characters are in a room with the narrator. How many characters' thoughts can the narrator tell you for sure?
practice.hint: Whose thoughts does a first-person narrator really know?
practice.explain: Only 1: the narrator's own. The other {n} characters' thoughts can only be guessed.

practice.prompt: A sentence has {a} narrator words (like I, me, my) and {b} pronouns inside speech marks. How many words change when you retell it in third person?
practice.hint: Speech stays exactly as it was said. Only the narrator's words change.
practice.explain: Only the {a} narrator words change. The {b} pronouns inside speech marks stay, because that is what the character said.

practice.prompt: An author wants you to know what both the hero and the villain are thinking. Which narrator fits best?
practice.hint: Which narrator can see inside more than one head?
practice.explain: An all-knowing third-person narrator can show every mind. A first-person narrator only knows their own.

choices: We hid behind the shed until dark.
They hid behind the shed until dark.
"We should hide," said Jo, and she ran.
pool.hint: Find a narrator word like I or we outside speech marks.
pool.explain: We, outside speech marks, includes the narrator. The third sentence has we only inside speech.

pool.prompt: Change "I dropped my phone" into third person about Raj.
pool.hint: Change every narrator word: I and my.
pool.explain: I becomes Raj and my becomes his. Changing only one word mixes two narrators.

pool.prompt: Sam and Mrs Patel both tell the window story. Why are their details different?
choices: Each chooses what matters to them
One of them made it all up
Stories have only one true version
pool.hint: Think about what each person cares about.
pool.explain: Sam tells about the wind and his worry. Mrs Patel tells about her curtains and that he ran off. Each narrator chooses.

pool.prompt: Why might an author choose first person for a diary story?
choices: It hides who the main character is
pool.hint: Who writes a diary, and how does it sound?
pool.explain: A diary is written by I. First person puts you inside the writer's head, so their feelings feel close.

pool.prompt: An all-knowing narrator tells a story about {n} friends. How many friends' thoughts can this narrator show?
pool.hint: An all-knowing narrator can see inside every head.
pool.explain: All {n}. An all-knowing third-person narrator can show any character's thoughts.

pool.prompt: Is the narrator always the author?
choices: No, the author chooses a narrator
pool.hint: Can a grown-up author write as a 10-year-old boy saying I?
pool.explain: The author writes the book. The narrator is the voice the author chooses to tell it, often a character.

pool.prompt: "I'll win," thought Mia. Which narrator is telling this?
pool.hint: Outside the quote, the narrator writes thought Mia, not I thought.
pool.explain: The narrator says thought Mia, so it is third person. It shows Mia's thoughts, so it follows her closely.

pool.prompt: A story has {a} chapters told by Ella and {b} chapters told by Ben, both in first person. How many narrators does it have?
pool.hint: Count the different voices saying I.
pool.explain: 2 narrators: Ella and Ben. The {a} + {b} chapters switch between their two points of view.
